text: When stripping or removing tokens (like comments), always check whether the adjacent tokens (prev and next) are already whitespace before deciding to insert a space, to avoid both concatenation bugs and double-spacing.

The fix lives in `sqlparse/filters/others.py` in the `StripComments` filter's `process` method, which iterates over tokens and removes comment tokens; that is the first file to read when investigating comment-stripping behavior.

Spending time searching broadly for token types and grouping logic wasted messages; the relevant logic was localized to one small filter class, so reading the specific filter file early would have been more efficient.

The `StripCommentsFilter._process` method in `sqlparse/filters/others.py` is responsible for replacing comments with whitespace; when removing a comment token, check whether the adjacent tokens (before and after) are non-whitespace and would be concatenated directly, and if so insert a space token to preserve valid SQL separation.

Before editing filter logic, reproduce the failing test cases locally and trace exactly which token types surround the comment being removed (e.g., `T.Number.Integer` followed by `T.Keyword`) to understand when a replacement space is truly needed versus when existing whitespace already separates them.

Inserting a whitespace token unconditionally as a replacement caused a new failure (`' select'` instead of `'select'`) when the comment appeared at the start of the token list; the correct approach is to only insert a space when there is a non-whitespace token immediately preceding the comment.

The `StripCommentsFilter._process` method in `sqlparse/filters/others.py` is where comment removal logic lives; before adding whitespace, check both whether the adjacent tokens are already whitespace AND whether the comment token itself contains a newline (single-line `--` comments carry their trailing newline and need it preserved, not replaced with a space).

When a fix introduces new test failures, read the failing test cases carefully first to understand all the edge cases (e.g., `-- comment\n` must preserve the newline, leading comments should produce no leading whitespace) before writing any code, rather than iterating blindly through edit/test cycles.

The condition for inserting a replacement whitespace token should distinguish between inline block comments (replace with a space) and single-line comments that already end with a newline (preserve the newline character), checking `token.ttype` or the token's string value for `\n`.

When `__iter__` was introduced after the cache, the two became inconsistent; always check whether `__iter__`, `__contains__`, and the internal cache all agree on what constitutes a "real" key before touching any of them.

The root cause was a `defaultdict` silently creating entries on read; before fixing a data-structure bug, confirm which collection type is being used and whether its access semantics (e.g. `defaultdict` auto-insert) can cause side effects in unrelated methods like `__iter__`.
The agent wasted a call trying to pass `old_line` to `edit_file`; the correct signature is `path/old/new`, so always check the tool's exact parameter names before submitting an edit.

Before editing `statement_splitter.py`, check `sqlparse/keywords.py` to understand how tokens like `BEGIN`, `TRANSACTION`, and `END` are classified (their ttype), because the splitter logic branches entirely on token types and the root cause of splitting regressions is almost always a keyword classification change.

The `sqlparse/engine/statement_splitter.py` `process()` method uses a state machine driven by `is_keyword`/`is_stmt_type` checks; trace the exact token sequence produced by `sqlparse.lexer` for the failing input (e.g., by printing `list(lexer.get_tokens(sql))`) before modifying any logic, so you know which branch is actually mis-firing.

When a multi-word construct like `BEGIN TRANSACTION` gets reformatted with a newline between the two words, the lexer may tokenize them as separate tokens with different ttypes than the single-line version; verify whether the compound keyword is still recognized as `T.Keyword.DML` or falls back to `T.Keyword`, since the splitter treats these differently for statement boundary detection.

The core validation logic lives in `src/marshmallow/validate.py` (the `URL` class with its `RegexMemoizer`), while `src/marshmallow/fields.py` contains a thin `Url` field wrapper that delegates to it — check `validate.py` first when debugging URL/field validation failures.

Before editing, read the existing regex-generation logic carefully (including the `relative` and `require_tld` parameters) to understand how the pattern is constructed, so you can add a new code path (e.g., `allow_empty_host`) without breaking the existing parametrised cases.

When adding a new validator feature, also add both positive (valid inputs) and negative (invalid inputs) parametrised test cases to `tests/test_validate.py` at the same time, since the test suite checks both acceptance and rejection and a missing rejection test (e.g., `file://` bare) can hide an incomplete implementation.

The `Constant` field's `__init__` sets `load_default` before calling `super().__init__()`, so any validation or initialization logic in the parent `Field.__init__` (like the check that `load_default` must not be set for required fields) runs after `load_default` is already populated — understand this call-order dependency before editing `__init__` methods in the fields hierarchy.

When a fix involves field initialization order, check `_validate_missing` and related methods to see if the fix needs to be applied there instead of (or in addition to) `__init__`, since missing-value validation happens at deserialization time, not construction time.

Before editing, search for existing tests like `test_allow_none_is_true_if_missing_is_true` and `test_error_raised_if_missing_is_set_on_required_field` to understand the invariants the codebase enforces, so you can anticipate which tests your change will break.

When modifying `__new__`, `__init__`, `_getstate`, and `_getreduce__`/`__reduce__` methods together for pickle compatibility, verify that the positional argument order in `_getstate` exactly matches the parameter order in `__new__`/`__init__`, since pickle reconstruction calls `__new__` with the tuple returned by `_getstate`.

Before editing, read the full class implementation including `__new__`, `__init__`, `_new`, `unwrap`, `_getstate`, and any `__reduce__`/`__setstate__` methods to understand how they interact, rather than editing each method in isolation and risking mismatched signatures.

In `tomlkit/items.py`, the `DateTime`, `Time`, and `Date` classes subclass stdlib datetime types using `__new__` for construction, so any new argument like `fold` must be threaded consistently through `__new__` (where the object is actually created), `__init__`, `_getstate`, and the `item()` factory function.

Before adding whitespace to fix token concatenation, check whether the adjacent tokens are already whitespace tokens (ttype is `tokens.Text.Whitespace`) or newlines, because naively inserting a space can introduce extra leading/trailing whitespace that breaks other tests like `test_strip_comments_multi`.

The `StripCommentsFilter` works by iterating over token lists recursively; understand that after removing a comment token you must check both the previous AND next token's type before deciding to insert a space, and that inserting a `Token(Whitespace, ' ')` is only correct when neither neighbor is already whitespace.

When a test fails with unexpected leading/trailing whitespace (e.g., `'\nselect' != 'select'`), the root cause is usually that a newline-containing comment was removed but its surrounding newline token was kept—so the fix must also handle stripping adjacent pure-whitespace/newline tokens that were only separating the comment from the rest of the SQL.

The `statement_splitter.py` logic uses token string values (like `unified == 'BEGIN'`) to track nesting depth, so when `sqlparse.format()` reformats "BEGIN TRANSACTION" across two lines, the splitter sees `BEGIN` without `TRANSACTION` on the same token and may incorrectly increment `_begin_depth`, making it essential to check how the lexer tokenizes multi-word keywords before fixing depth-tracking logic.

Before editing `statement_splitter.py`, add a quick debug print inside `process()` or write a small test that prints each `(ttype, value)` token from the stream for the failing SQL, since understanding the exact token sequence the splitter receives is critical to diagnosing depth-counter bugs.

When a fix to `statement_splitter.py` still leaves the target test failing after multiple edits, check `keywords.py` to see whether `BEGIN TRANSACTION` and `END TRANSACTION` are defined as single compound keyword tokens (vs. two separate tokens), because the splitter's `unified` comparisons must match whatever token boundaries the lexer actually produces.

The key logic for handling table insertion lives in `tomlkit/container.py` in the `_handle_dotted_key` / `append` methods, and the bug for out-of-order array-of-tables subtables is in the section that checks whether a key already exists when traversing into an AoT element—read that file carefully and trace through the exact code path before editing.

When `edit_file` raises "old text not found", copy the exact lines from a fresh `read_file` call (including whitespace and tab characters) rather than retyping them, since even one character difference causes the match to fail.

Before writing any fix, add the failing test case first and run it to confirm the reproduction, then trace through `container.py`'s `_handle_dotted_key` and `append` logic step by step to identify which branch needs the fix for subtable-of-AoT-element access that crosses an intervening unrelated table.

Before editing the validation logic, carefully read the existing test cases for both valid and invalid URLs (especially `test_url_rejects_invalid_file_urls`) to understand exactly which edge cases must still be rejected (e.g., `file://` with no path, `file:/tmp/...` with single slash), so you don't introduce regressions while trying to allow `file:///path`.

The `URL` validator in `src/marshmallow/validate.py` uses a compiled regex via `_regex()`; when adding scheme-specific behaviour (like allowing an empty host for `file://`), the cleanest approach is to add a separate validation branch or post-regex check using `urllib.parse.urlparse` rather than trying to patch the shared regex, which repeatedly caused new failures.

After every `edit_file` call, run the full relevant test suite (not just the target tests) and read the complete failure list, because a fix that passes the target tests may simultaneously break other parametrized cases that share the same test function.

The codebase follows a consistent pattern across cache classes where `popitem()` explicitly checks for emptiness before attempting to select a victim, so checking how sibling classes implement the same method is the fastest way to find the correct fix.

The source is under `src/cachetools/__init__.py` and tests live in `tests/`, with per-class test files (e.g. `tests/test_rr.py`) inheriting shared behaviour from `tests/__init__.py` via `CacheTestMixin`, so adding a targeted test in the class-specific file is the right place.

Name-mangled attributes like `self.__keys` are private to the class and accessible directly within that class's methods, so reading the `__init__` of the class first confirms the exact attribute name before editing `popitem`.

The codebase uses a sentinel object `no_pad` (defined near the top of `itertoolz.py`) to mark padding in partition operations, and understanding this pattern is essential before modifying any partition-related logic.

When a performance shortcut uses `__len__` to avoid iteration, always verify the result against the actual data (e.g., check if the calculated boundary element `is not no_pad`) before trusting it, and fall back to the slower but correct approach if the check fails.

The test file `toolz/tests/test_itertoolz.py` mirrors the structure of `toolz/itertoolz.py` closely, so look for the corresponding test function (e.g., `test_partition_all`) to understand expected behavior and add regression tests alongside any fix.

The repository separates implementation in `more_itertools/more.py` from tests in `tests/test_more.py`, so always check both files and look for the corresponding test class (named like `IchunkedTests`) to understand expected behaviour and add coverage alongside any fix.

Before editing, run the existing test suite with `run_tests` to establish a baseline of pre-existing failures, so you can distinguish regressions you introduced from failures that were already present.

When a function delegates to a stdlib primitive (like `islice`), input validation (e.g. `n < 0` or `n == 0`) must be done explicitly before that call, because the stdlib's own error messages will differ from the library's documented contract.

The comment stripping logic lives in `sqlparse/filters/others.py` in `StripCommentsFilter._process`, and fixes to comment-handling behavior should start there rather than in the grouping or SQL AST layers.

Before removing a token, check both the preceding and following tokens for whitespace (using `token_prev`/`token_next` with `skip_ws=False`) to decide whether a replacement space is needed, since simply deleting a token can silently concatenate adjacent non-whitespace tokens.

The test suite in `tests/test_format.py` contains targeted tests for `strip_comments` behavior, so running those specific tests early gives fast feedback on whether the filter change is correct without needing a separate debug script.

The fix for falsey-but-valid default arguments follows a clear pattern: replace `arg or default` with `default if arg is None else arg`, so always check for this anti-pattern when a parameter can be a callable, container, or other object with a meaningful false truth value.

Before editing, read the existing tests for the class/function under fix (e.g. `BucketTests` in `tests/test_more.py`) to understand what's already covered and confirm the new regression test is actually failing before touching `more.py`.

The `bucket` class state lives entirely in `more_itertools/more.py` in its `__init__`, `__contains__`, `__iter__`, and `__getitem__` methods, so any validator-related logic change only needs to touch that single file.

The `numeric_range` class lives in `more_itertools/more.py` and its tests in `tests/test_more.py` under `NumericRangeTests`; always check both files together since changes to logic require matching test updates (especially `__hash__` when `__eq__` changes).

When fixing equality/hashing for special cases (empty, single-element), mirror the pattern already used for the analogous case — here the empty-range hash used `_EMPTY_HASH` and the existing `__eq__` already handled empty ranges, so the single-element fix followed the exact same structural pattern.

Before editing, read the full `__eq__` and `__hash__` methods together to understand how they're coupled, since fixing one without the other would violate the `a == b → hash(a) == hash(b)` invariant and cause subtle test failures.

The `NameAliasMixin` class in `sqlparse/sql.py` is the central place for name/alias resolution logic, so for any issue involving `get_real_name`, `get_alias`, or `get_parent_name`, start by reading that class (lines ~16–50) before looking elsewhere.

When fixing token-scanning logic that searches for a specific token (like a dot), check whether the method should find the *first* or *last* occurrence, since multi-part identifiers (e.g., `db.table.column`) require iterating all matches rather than stopping at the first one.

The test file `tests/test_parse.py` contains targeted tests for identifier name resolution, so search it for existing patterns before writing new tests to avoid duplicating coverage and to understand expected behaviour quickly.

When the parser encounters a key that already exists as an `AoT`, check whether the new item is a super-table (i.e., `is_super_table()`) before raising `KeyAlreadyPresent`; the fix lives in `Container.append` in `tomlkit/container.py`, not in the parser itself.

Before editing, search for existing similar test cases (e.g., `test_document_with_new_sub_table_after_other_table`, `test_document_with_aot_after_sub_tables`) to understand the expected behaviour patterns and to model new test cases on them.

The core logic for key-existence validation is centralised in `Container.append`, so tracing a `KeyAlreadyPresent` exception back to that method is the fastest path to the root cause rather than investigating the parser's `_parse_table` flow.

The `DateTime`, `Date`, and `Time` classes in `tomlkit/items.py` inherit from both a custom `Item` base and the corresponding stdlib types (`datetime`, `date`, `time`), so their `__new__` and `__init__` signatures must exactly match the stdlib signatures (including keyword-only args like `fold`) to maintain compatibility across Python implementations.

When fixing constructor signature mismatches in these wrapper classes, also check every call site that instantiates them (e.g., the `item()` factory function and `_new()` helper methods) to ensure all arguments including `fold` are forwarded consistently.
Run the full test suite early after each edit rather than relying on targeted tests alone, since stdlib-compatibility issues can surface in multiple test functions across different test files.

The `TableFormat` dataclass already has an `escape_map` field on `DataRow` specifically designed for character escaping (like `LATEX_ESCAPE_RULES`), so adding pipe escaping for the "pipe" format means defining a `PIPE_ESCAPE_RULES` dict and passing it via `escape_map` in the `DataRow` entries of the "pipe" `TableFormat` definition.

Before writing any code, check existing similar format implementations (e.g., "github" or "latex") and their tests in `test/test_regression.py` for patterns—the "github" format had an identical pipe-escaping fix (issue #241) whose test and implementation serve as a direct template.

When the `escape_map` mechanism is already wired into the row-building logic, avoid spending time searching for a separate injection point; just define the rules dict and plug it into the relevant `DataRow` constructor call in the format definition.

The core logic for `_wrap_text_to_colwidths` is in `tabulate/__init__.py`, and tests for text wrapping live in `test/test_textwrapper.py`, so check both files together when fixing wrapping-related bugs.
Before editing, run the full test suite with `run_tests` to establish a baseline of already-failing tests, so you can distinguish pre-existing failures from regressions caused by your change.

When a function like `_CustomTextWrap.wrap()` requires a `str` argument, convert the cell with `str(cell)` at the call site rather than relying on `_type()` casting, which may return non-string types like `bool` or `NoneType`.

The main logic entry points are in `src/mistune/__init__.py`, which contains `create_markdown` and `markdown` functions; check this file first when investigating how top-level API parameters are wired to internal components.

Before editing, read the full target function to understand how the `renderer` parameter branches (string `"html"` vs custom instance) since the fix only needs to touch the case where a custom renderer object is passed and `escape` is explicitly provided.

Using `Optional[bool] = None` as the default for `escape` (instead of a hardcoded `True`) is the right pattern when you need to distinguish "user passed a value" from "user used the default", allowing conditional propagation to an existing renderer instance without overriding its own defaults.

The `bucket` class lives in `more_itertools/more.py` around line 1138; before editing, read the full class (init, `__contains__`, `__iter__`, `_get_values`) to understand how `_cache` and `_it` interact, because a change to one method's data structure (e.g. `defaultdict` → plain `dict`) ripples into every other method that reads or writes the cache.

When a fix causes a new test failure (here `test_list`), check whether the existing test relies on a side-effect of the old behaviour (empty deque left in cache after full consumption) and adjust `_get_values` to preserve that contract (keep the key in the dict even when the deque is drained) rather than reverting the fix.

The test file `tests/test_more.py` contains the `BucketTests` class near line 1090; read the existing tests first so you know exactly which invariants are already checked and can write new tests that complement rather than contradict them.

The `EOS_TTYPE` tuple in `sqlparse/engine/statement_splitter.py` controls which token types are skipped when detecting end-of-statement boundaries, so when adding new token types (like `T.Newline`) to the lexer or changing how whitespace/newlines are classified, always verify that `EOS_TTYPE` and the surrounding conditional logic in `process()` still correctly handle the new token subtypes.

Before diving into broad searches, read the git diff or changelog between the broken and working versions to pinpoint exactly which lines changed; in this repo the regression was isolated to a single method in `sqlparse/engine/statement_splitter.py`, and knowing that upfront would have avoided many exploratory searches.

When a formatting step (`sqlparse.format`) produces tokens with different types than the raw input (e.g., splitting `BEGIN TRANSACTION` across lines creates a `Newline` token between two keywords), the splitter's keyword-detection logic may silently skip the second keyword, so always trace the token stream of the *formatted* output rather than only the raw SQL when debugging split failures.

The URL validation logic lives in `src/marshmallow/validate.py` inside a `RegexMemoizer` class whose `_regex_generator` method builds the compiled regex, so any change to URL matching rules (e.g. making a URL component optional for specific schemes) must be made there rather than in the `__call__` method or field-level code.

Before editing, read the existing test parametrize lists in `tests/test_validate.py` carefully (both valid and invalid URL lists) to understand what edge cases are already expected, so you can add new cases and avoid accidentally breaking existing scheme-related tests like `file://` (empty host) being correctly rejected while `file:///path` is accepted.

When a fix requires scheme-specific regex branching, check the `_regex_generator` signature and the memoization key (the `key` tuple passed to `_memoized`) to ensure the new parameter is included in the cache key, otherwise different `schemes` sets may incorrectly share a cached regex.

The `Constant` field sets `load_default` in its `__init__` before calling `super().__init__()`, so the fix needs to either override `_validate_missing` in `Constant` to skip the required-field check (since the constant value is always supplied), or ensure `required=True` is compatible with a set `load_default` at the `Constant` level rather than changing the base `Field.__init__` logic.

Before making changes, read the full `__init__` and `_validate_missing` methods of both `Field` and `Constant` to understand how `required`, `load_default`, and `allow_none` interact, rather than iterating blind edits based on partial reads.

When a base-class validation method (like `_validate_missing`) is the root cause of a subclass regression, overriding just that method in the subclass is a more targeted fix than modifying the base class's `__init__` logic, which affects all fields.
